entry.title: Edition 5: Ludwig Wittgenstein
entry.summary: “Philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language.” — Ludwig Wittgenstein, Philosophical Investigations (§109 (1953)). Question: Pick a word you use daily without hesitation—'freedom', 'self', 'success'. Where does it stop meaning anything definite when you press on it?

entry.title: Rationalism vs. Empiricism
entry.summary: In its most general terms, the distinction between rationalism and empiricism has been taken to concern the extent to which we are dependent upon experience in our effort to gain knowledge of the external world. Experience includes both sense experience, which comes through our five outward-directed sense modalities, and reflective experience, our conscious awareness of mental activities such as thinking, doubting, remembering, and reasoning.

entry.title: A Game for Teaching Ancient Philosophy
entry.summary: The game is set around 150 BCE at the court of Menander, a king who ruled a Hellenistic kingdom that included part of the Indian subcontinent. Four delegations of philosophers (Stoics, Epicureans, Buddhists, and Skeptics) arrive at court, each claiming to offer the best way of life. There is no predetermined winner: when I ran the game in two sections of my ethics course, different philosophical factions won.

entry.title: What the End of Anonymous Writing Means for Academia
entry.summary: Large language models are getting increasingly good at identifying the authors of human-written text. The authors asked LLMs to provide the identity of different kinds of often-anonymous writing, such as peer reviews and internet comments. Moreover, the set of vulnerable writers expands as models improve… Maintaining anonymity is especially important for peer review.
